\section{Introduction}
\subsection{Legendre Polynomials}
Let $P_k(x)$ be the degree $k$ Legendre polynomial. The Legendre polynomials
are an orthogonal family of polynomials on $[-1,1]$ that obey the orthogonality
relation
$$
\int_{-1}^1 P_j(x) P_k(x) dx = 0,
$$
for $j \not = k$. The first few Legendre polynomials are
$$
P_0(x) = 1, \qquad P_1(x) = x, \qquad \text{and} \qquad P_2(x) = \frac{3 x^2 - 1}{2}.  
$$
The Legendre polynomials obey the recurrence relation
$$
(k+1) P_{k+1}(x) = (2 k + 1) x P_k(x) - k P_{k-1}(x),
$$
the differential equation
$$
(1 - x^2) P_k''(x) - 2 x P_k'(x) + k(k+1) P_k(x) = 0,
$$
for $k \ge 1$.

        \textit{Exact:} & If $ M(x,y) + N(x,y)dy/dx = 0 $ and $ M_y = N_x $ i.e. $ \langle M,N \rangle = \nabla F $ then $ \int_x M + \int_y N = F $ \\ \hline
        \textit{Order Reduction} & Let $ v = dy/dx $ then check other types \\ 
        &\textit{If purely a function of y, }$\frac{dv}{dx} = v\frac{dv}{dy}$\\
        \hline
        \textit{Variation of Parameters:} & When $y''+a_1y'+a_2y = F(x)$ \\
        & $F$ contains $\ln x$, $\sec x$, $\tan x$, $\div$ \\ \hline
        \textit{Bernoulli} & $y' + P(x)y = Q(x)y^n$ \\
        & $\div y^n$ \\
        &$y^{-n}y'+P(x)y^{1-n}=Q(x)$ \textit{Let }$U(x) = y^{1-n}(x)$ \\
        &$\frac{dU}{dx}=(1-n)y^{-n}\frac{dy}{dx}$ \\
        &$\frac{1}{1-n}\frac{du}{dx} + P(x)U(x) = Q(x)$ \textit{solve as a 1st order} \\ \hline
        \textit{Cauchy-Euler} &$x^ny^n + a_1x^{n-1}y^{n-1} + \cdots + a_{n-1}y^{n-2}+a_ny = 0$ \\

        \textit{2) Repeated real roots} &$y = Ax^r + y_2$ \\
        &\textit{Guess} $y_2 = x^ru(x)$ \\

\miquestion
\begin{parts}
  \part Define what it means for a finite subset of a vector space to be
  {\em linearly independent}, a {\em spanning set}, and a {\em basis}.

  State the {\it Steinitz Exchange Lemma}.

  Prove that if a vector space $V$ has a finite basis, then every linearly
  independent subset of $V$ may be extended to a basis.

  Prove that any two finite bases of a vector space have the same number of
  elements. Define the {\em dimension} of a finite-dimensional vector space.

  \part Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space.

  Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are subspaces of $V$.

  Prove that
  \[ \dim(X+Y)+\dim(X\cap Y)=\dim X+\dim Y. \]

  \part Suppose $V$ is a finite-dimensional vector space, and $T:V\to V $
  is a linear transformation. Suppose that for all $v\in V$, if $T(T(v))=0$,
  then $T(v)=0$. Prove that $V=\ker T\oplus \mathop{\rm im} T$, and that the
  restriction, $T{\restriction} {\mathop{\rm im} T}$, of $T$ to $\mathop{\rm
    im} T$ is a bijection from $\mathop{\rm im} T$ to itself.

  [{\em You may assume the Rank-Nullity Theorem.}]

    transformation,

    and $U$ is a subspace of $V$, then we define the {\em restriction}
    $T{\restriction} U$ of $T$ to $U$ to be a linear transformation from $U$
    to $W$ such that for all $u\in U$, $(T{\restriction} U)(u)=T(u)$.}]
\end{parts}

    entries is {\em diagonalisable} over ${\mathbb R}$.  \subpart Show that

    \subpart Consider the $2\times 2$ real square matrix

    \subpart Determine when the $2\times 2$ real matrix
    \[ A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\cr c&a\cr\end{pmatrix} \] is diagonalisable.
  \end{subparts}
\end{parts}

\miquestion Let $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ be vectors in
$\mathbb{R}^3$.
\begin{parts}
  \part[7]
  \begin{subparts}
    \subpart Prove that $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ are linearly
    independent if and only if 
    $\mathbf{u}.(\mathbf{v}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{w})\neq \mathbf{0}$.  
    \subpart Establish the identity
    \[
    \mathbf{u}\mathbin{\land}(\mathbf{w}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{v})
    =(\mathbf{u}.\mathbf{v})\mathbf{w}-(\mathbf{u}.\mathbf{w})\mathbf{v}.
    \]
  \end{subparts}

  \part[7] Prove that $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ are linearly
  independent if and only if
  $\mathbf{v}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{w}$, 
  $\mathbf{w}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{u}$, and
  $\mathbf{u}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{v}$ are linearly independent.

  \part[6] Suppose that $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ are
  linearly independent, and that
  \[ \mathbf{r}=a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v}+c\mathbf{w}. \]
  Find coefficients $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ such that
  \[
  \mathbf{r}=\alpha\mathbf{v}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{w}
  +\beta\mathbf{w}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{u}
  +\gamma\mathbf{u}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{v}.
  \]

\end{parts}

    \textbf{iii. Identity:} $\exists$ e $\in$ G, called an identity of G,\\ s.t. $\forall$ a $\in$ G we have a * e = e * a = a\\

§ INTRODUCTION

A popular tool for evaluating generative models is the classifier two-sample
test (C2ST). It reframes distributional comparison between p(x) and q(x) as
a classification task over the space , with the Bayes-optimal classifier
bisecting ^2 between the two means.



  
Summary of contributions. We introduce the Conformal C2ST and give
a robustness theory for weak classifiers. We show that conformal calibration
decouples type-I error control from discriminative accuracy.



  
A toy example. Consider (0, I_2) versus a mean shift,
so that q is ([0.5, 0]^⊤, I_2). The rank statistic

    r = ∑_i=1^M{θ≤θ̃_i}

in:
\section{Robustness of the uniform test}
Let $\cO$ denote an oracle and write the conformal $p$-value as a function of
the score. We control the variance $\var[r]$ and the expectation $\EE[r]$ of
the rank statistic under the null.

\begin{theorem}[Decoupling]
\label{thm:decouple}
For any plug-in classifier with score $s$, the conformal calibration map
satisfies
\[
  \Big| \EE\big[ \phi(s) \big] - \alpha \Big| \le \norm{s - s^\star}
  \xrightarrow{\;n \to \infty\;} 0 ,
\]
where $s^\star$ is the Bayes-optimal score and $\abs{\alpha} \le 1$.
\end{theorem}

As shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:decouple}, the conformal test maintains validity
even when the classifier is weak, since the ranking signal
$\overset{\text{rank}}{\longrightarrow}$ aggregates across draws.

§ INTRODUCTION



 §.§ Legendre Polynomials

Let P_k(x) be the degree k Legendre polynomial. The Legendre polynomials
are an orthogonal family of polynomials on [-1,1] that obey the orthogonality
relation

    ∫_-1^1 P_j(x) P_k(x) dx = 0,

for j ≠ k. The first few Legendre polynomials are

    P_0(x) = 1,      P_1(x) = x,     and     P_2(x) = 3 x^2 - 1/2.

The Legendre polynomials obey the recurrence relation

    (k+1) P_k+1(x) = (2 k + 1) x P_k(x) - k P_k-1(x),

the differential equation

    (1 - x^2) P_k”(x) - 2 x P_k'(x) + k(k+1) P_k(x) = 0,

for k ≥ 1.

\section{Introduction}
\subsection{Legendre Polynomials}
Let $P_k(x)$ be the degree $k$ Legendre polynomial. The Legendre polynomials
are an orthogonal family of polynomials on $[-1,1]$ that obey the orthogonality
relation
$$
\int_{-1}^1 P_j(x) P_k(x) dx = 0,
$$
for $j \not = k$. The first few Legendre polynomials are
$$
P_0(x) = 1, \qquad P_1(x) = x, \qquad \text{and} \qquad P_2(x) = \frac{3 x^2 - 1}{2}.  
$$
The Legendre polynomials obey the recurrence relation
$$
(k+1) P_{k+1}(x) = (2 k + 1) x P_k(x) - k P_{k-1}(x),
$$
the differential equation
$$
(1 - x^2) P_k''(x) - 2 x P_k'(x) + k(k+1) P_k(x) = 0,
$$
for $k \ge 1$.

 §.§ Part a)


√(2) is irrational.


Suppose that √(2) were rational. There there exist some non-zero integers p and q such that 
    √(2) = p/q.
 Without loss of generality, we can assume that this fraction is simplified so that p and q have no common divisors. Then,

    √(2)q    = p 
    
        2q^2   = p^2.

This implies (by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic) that 2 divides p^2 and, hence, 2 divides p. Therefore, p = 2r for some (non-zero) integer r. Therefore,

    2q^2   = p^2
    
        2q^2   = (2r)^2
    
        2q^2   = 4r^2
    
        q^2   = 2r^2.

From this, we conclude that 2 divides q^2 and, hence, 2 divides q. This is a contradiction as we assumed p and q were written so that they share no common divisors (other than the trivial divisor 1, of course). Therefore, √(2) is not a rational number.

\begin{questions}

\miquestion
\begin{parts}
  \part Define what it means for a finite subset of a vector space to be
  {\em linearly independent}, a {\em spanning set}, and a {\em basis}.

  State the {\it Steinitz Exchange Lemma}.

  Prove that if a vector space $V$ has a finite basis, then every linearly
  independent subset of $V$ may be extended to a basis.

  Prove that any two finite bases of a vector space have the same number of
  elements. Define the {\em dimension} of a finite-dimensional vector space.

  \part Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space.

  Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are subspaces of $V$.

  Prove that
  \[ \dim(X+Y)+\dim(X\cap Y)=\dim X+\dim Y. \]

  \part Suppose $V$ is a finite-dimensional vector space, and $T:V\to V $
  is a linear transformation. Suppose that for all $v\in V$, if $T(T(v))=0$,
  then $T(v)=0$. Prove that $V=\ker T\oplus \mathop{\rm im} T$, and that the
  restriction, $T{\restriction} {\mathop{\rm im} T}$, of $T$ to $\mathop{\rm
    im} T$ is a bijection from $\mathop{\rm im} T$ to itself.

  [{\em You may assume the Rank-Nullity Theorem.}]

  [{\em If\/ $V$ and $W$ are vector spaces, $T:V\to W$ is a linear
    transformation,

    and $U$ is a subspace of $V$, then we define the {\em restriction}
    $T{\restriction} U$ of $T$ to $U$ to be a linear transformation from $U$
    to $W$ such that for all $u\in U$, $(T{\restriction} U)(u)=T(u)$.}]
\end{parts}

\begin{solution}

\end{solution}

  matrix may be reduced to row-reduced echelon form.

          x&-2y&-5z&=&7\cr 2x&+8y&+(-\lambda-6)z&=&8\cr
          x&-2y&+(\lambda-3)z&=&\lambda^2+3\cr }}}}
  \]
\end{parts}

    entries is {\em diagonalisable} over ${\mathbb R}$.  \subpart Show that

    eigenvalues of $A$ corresponding to different eigenvalues, then $\bf u$
    and $\bf v$ are linearly independent.
  \end{subparts}

    least one real eigenvalue; and that if $a\neq d$ or $b\neq 0$, then it
    has two distinct real eigenvalues.

    Deduce that $A$ is diagonalisable.

    matrix
    \[ A=\begin{pmatrix}1&\alpha\cr \beta&1\cr\end{pmatrix} \] is
    diagonalisable.

    \subpart Determine when the $2\times 2$ real matrix
    \[ A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\cr c&a\cr\end{pmatrix} \] is diagonalisable.
  \end{subparts}
\end{parts}

\miquestion Let $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ be vectors in
$\mathbb{R}^3$.
\begin{parts}
  \part[7]
  \begin{subparts}
    \subpart Prove that $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ are linearly
    independent if and only if 
    $\mathbf{u}.(\mathbf{v}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{w})\neq \mathbf{0}$.  
    \subpart Establish the identity
    \[
    \mathbf{u}\mathbin{\land}(\mathbf{w}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{v})
    =(\mathbf{u}.\mathbf{v})\mathbf{w}-(\mathbf{u}.\mathbf{w})\mathbf{v}.
    \]
  \end{subparts}

  independent if and only if
  $\mathbf{v}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{w}$, 
  $\mathbf{w}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{u}$, and
  $\mathbf{u}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{v}$ are linearly independent.

  linearly independent, and that
  \[ \mathbf{r}=a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v}+c\mathbf{w}. \]
  Find coefficients $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ such that
  \[
  \mathbf{r}=\alpha\mathbf{v}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{w}
  +\beta\mathbf{w}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{u}
  +\gamma\mathbf{u}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{v}.
  \]

\end{parts}
